title: Hosted API: Live Chat Onramp — params, streaming, fault tolerance
summary: Intro demo covering chat/text generation basics on Redwood Hosted API: streaming behavior, key params to control token usage and style, and recommended retry/backoff strategies. SE did a brief console tour and suggested Optimize levers for cost and latency. Customer asked about PHI handling and VPC/private options; next step is security deck and a small pilot with 10k tokens/day sample workload.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Priya Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Elena Morris (Nimbus Health - CTO), Daniel Kwon (Nimbus - Lead ML Eng), Sana Farooqi (Nimbus - DevOps), Tom Reed (Nimbus - Product)

---
00:00 Speaker 1 (Priya): okay everyone good afternoon thanks for joining, really quick agenda: we’ll do a short hosted API demo, show streaming behavior, call out key generation params, and go over retry/backoff patterns. diego will jump into the console and an optimize note at the end. sound good?
00:12 Speaker 2 (Elena): sounds good, yeah we just want a clear onramp, we have some PHI concerns so if you can note where data rests that'd help.
00:20 Speaker 1 (Priya): absolutely, we’ll hit that in the security section. quick intro, nina, elena — sorry — elena thanks for joining, could you remind the team what your immediate use case is?
00:29 Speaker 3 (Elena): sure, we’re building a clinical notes summarization assistant for clinicians; low latency is important but we also need to avoid hallucinations and keep PHI in control. current stack: GKE, some on-prem postgres, and a fedramp-like compliance posture; thinking hosted first but may need private later.
00:48 Speaker 4 (Diego): got it. For hosted, we do configurable retention and optional Customer Data controls; private/VPC options are available when you hit the enterprise lane. ok i’ll pop into the console in a sec.
00:58 Speaker 2 (Elena): timeline is Q1 pilot, then maybe larger POC.
01:05 Speaker 1 (Priya): perfect. quick qual — target throughput and expected prompt sizes?
01:13 Speaker 3 (Elena): average prompt ~400 tokens, sometimes 2k with context, target concurrency ~30-50 requests per second during peak.
01:21 Speaker 4 (Diego): ok that’s helpful. so i’ll demo streaming and also show how parameters like max_tokens and temperature change behaviors and cost.
01:31 Speaker 5 (Tom): also curious about retries — if a stream dies mid-sentence how do we resume?
01:38 Speaker 4 (Diego): great question — we’ll show a couple patterns: idempotent request keys + chunk-aware reconnection, and fallback to a cheaper model for availability.

02:12 Speaker 4 (Diego): (screen) jumping into the Redwood Console -> Hosted API -> Models. here’s our chat endpoint example, we’ll switch to the streaming toggle. note: streaming sends incremental deltas over a socket or SSE; you can start rendering before the whole response completes. transcription note: sometimes SSE is labelled web sockets in the ui, minor naming fuzz.
02:36 Speaker 4 (Diego): code sample in the right panel — node snippet uses the stream param and an onDelta callback. snippet (rough): const stream = client.chat.stream({model: 'rwd-clarity-7b', messages, temperature: 0.1, max_tokens: 600}); stream.on('delta', d => render(d.text)); stream.on('error', e => handleRetry(e));
02:58 Speaker 4 (Diego): one thing to watch — max_tokens controls the output truncation and cost; if you set it too high for 2k contexts you’ll pay more even if you only need a short summary, so we recommend conservative max_tokens + stop sequences.
03:14 Speaker 2 (Daniel): on stop sequences — we have structured outputs, can you enforce JSON?
03:20 Speaker 4 (Diego): yes, structured output via functions or response schema works well. streaming + structured output is fine, you just buffer tokens until the schema completes, or you can validate on the fly. small caveat: if you use streaming and expect exact JSON you need to reassemble the deltas and run a final parse/validator.
03:38 Speaker 1 (Priya): quick question from procurement: data retention defaults in hosted?
03:43 Speaker 4 (Diego): default is short-term retention for telemetry; we offer opt-out of retention for enterprise and we can enable tenant-level KMS. for PHI, our recommendation is private deployment or dedicated pools with strict logging, and we have SOC 2+ controls. i’ll attach the security pack.
03:59 Speaker 2 (Elena): good.

04:18 Speaker 4 (Diego): moving to retries — typical failure modes: transient network, rate limit 429s, server-side preemption on heavy tails. recommended pattern: 1) client-side exponential backoff with jitter, 2) idempotency keys for safe retry, 3) stream resume where possible. example backoff: base 200ms, factor 2, max 8s, jitter 0.2.
04:45 Speaker 5 (Tom): if stream dies after partial response is that lost?
04:50 Speaker 4 (Diego): depends — with streaming you usually get deltas you rendered; we recommend persisting deltas server-side or using a request_id to ask for a flush/redo — Redwood also supports a sync endpoint (non-stream) to re-run a request to get the canonical full output.
05:05 Speaker 2 (Daniel): can we checkpoint KV-cache to resume with the same context?
05:11 Speaker 4 (Diego): KV cache is internal to the runtime for speed; you can snapshot conversation context at the application layer — we don’t expose the internal KV cache for security. but you can store the minimal context to replay.

06:02 Speaker 4 (Diego): demoing a failure scenar — i’ll simulate a dropped connection. (sfx: clicking) stream.connect -> stream.delta -> disconnect -> stream.error. client code: on error, attempt reconnect with last_stream_token and the request id. sometimes the token offset is noisy in transcriptions, i’ll type the snippet in chat.
06:28 Speaker 4 (Diego): here’s a restart helper: if (attempts < 3) backoff(); client.chat.stream({request_id, resume_from: offset}) — resume_from is app-level; the hosted API does not guarantee byte offsets but request_id + deterministic prompt will yield same output probabilistically.
06:47 Speaker 2 (Elena): is there a replay API that guarantees exact same tokens?
06:52 Speaker 4 (Diego): not strictly — nondeterminism in sampling means exact-token replay requires deterministic sampling (temperature 0, fixed seed) or a cached canonical output saved by your app. Redwood can pin model versions which increases determinism.
07:10 Speaker 1 (Priya): can you show the Optimize tab briefly — what levers would you recommend for a summarization workload?
07:18 Speaker 4 (Diego): sure. Optimize shows batching suggestions, cache prefixes, and quantization guidance. for summarization we typically recommend: lower temperature (0.0–0.2), small max_tokens for concise summaries, enable prefix caching for repeated patient metadata, and suggest a medium-sized model family (rwd-clarity-7b quantized) for cost/latency balance.
07:41 Speaker 5 (Tom): how about hallucination monitoring?
07:45 Speaker 4 (Diego): we tie evals to prompt sets; you can upload prompts and expected outputs and run periodic regression alerts. also suggest a reranker step if you need precision — generate candidates then rerank against a verification prompt.

08:20 Speaker 3 (Elena): quick interjection — on compliance, is SSO/SAML and RBAC available for hosted customers?
08:26 Speaker 4 (Diego): yes SSO + SAML and role-based access controls on the Console. audit logs are available for enterprise. for strict PHI, private deployment recommended.

09:00 Speaker 4 (Diego): live code demo — here’s a node + python snippet for streaming + reconnect. (reads code) note: include idempotency key = user_id + timestamp truncated; avoid including raw PHI in keys. there’s also a sample bash script in our repo for automatic backoff retries. i’ll paste links in the follow-up.
09:35 Speaker 2 (Daniel): can you show token accounting — how do we project cost?
09:40 Speaker 4 (Diego): Console -> Usage -> Token breakdown. you can filter by model, route, and tag. Optimize will estimate cost per 1k tokens with given batching. for your expected 400 token prompts at 50 rps that’s a rough calc — we can run a model-level perf estimate in the pilot.
10:05 Speaker 1 (Priya): question from legal folks: data residency for EU patients?
10:10 Speaker 4 (Diego): we have region pinning and can restrict data to eu-west runs; for stronger controls private deployment on customer infra is the option.
10:18 Speaker 2 (Sana): Ops question: what about autoscaling — cold starts bad for latency?
10:23 Speaker 4 (Diego): Dedicated pools with reserved capacity reduce cold starts; autoscaling policies support warm pools and burst capacity. for strict latency SLOs we recommend committed dedicated instance reservations.

11:02 Speaker 4 (Diego): one tip: prefer batching at the app layer where you can, and set max_batch_latency to tune user-visible delay. another tip: use token-level streaming to render partial content for clinicians while final verification runs.
11:28 Speaker 5 (Tom): any gotchas with stop tokens vs truncation?
11:33 Speaker 4 (Diego): stop tokens will end generation early; truncation via max_tokens may cut off mid-structure so use stop sequences where possible for structured outputs.

12:15 Speaker 1 (Priya): okay let’s surface a few narrow follow-ups — Diego will share code and security pack; i’ll send pricing and pilot options. any other questions?
12:26 Speaker 3 (Elena): can you include a sample config that targets 50 rps and 4k context? that will help our infra planning.
12:33 Speaker 4 (Diego): yes will include a sample throughput.cfg and a bench script.
12:40 Speaker 2 (Daniel): also please confirm if logs can be truncated to remove PHI before storage — we need retention policy controls.
12:47 Speaker 4 (Diego): yes we have ingestion hooks; can redact at edge and we can discuss retention in the security doc.
12:55 Speaker 1 (Priya): excellent. recap of next steps: security pack + pricing (Priya), streaming SDK + reconnect patterns (Diego), customer provides sample prompts & traffic profile (Daniel). we’ll aim to kick off a 2-week pilot the week of 2026-12-14.
13:15 Speaker 3 (Elena): thanks everyone.
13:18 Speaker 1 (Priya): thanks all, ending now.
